shorts.title: Warren Buffett's $200 Billion Revenge Mistake
shorts.description: The greatest investor alive bought a dying textile company out of spite. He later called it a $200 billion mistake.

scenes.text: The greatest investor in the world made a two hundred billion dollar mistake… out of pride.
In the early sixties, Warren Buffett was buying shares of a textile company called Berkshire Hathaway.
The boss promised to buy his shares back at one price, then offered a little less.
Buffett was so angry, he bought control of the whole company and fired him.
But it was a dying textile business. Buffett later said that revenge cost him around two hundred billion dollars.
Lesson: never invest angry.

shorts.title: He Lost £500 Million With One Joke
shorts.description: In 1991, Gerald Ratner called his own products 'crap' in a speech. His company never recovered.
sources: Wikipedia: Gerald Ratner — Institute of Directors speech, April 1991

scenes.text: This man destroyed his own company with one joke.
In 1991, Gerald Ratner ran the biggest jewelry chain in Britain.
In a speech, he joked that some of his products were total crap.
His customers heard it. And they stopped buying.
About five hundred million pounds was wiped off the company's value, and Ratner was soon out.
In Britain, it's still called doing a Ratner. Careful what you say.

shorts.title: The Record Label That Rejected The Beatles 🎸
shorts.description: On January 1, 1962, Decca Records auditioned The Beatles and said no.

scenes.text: On New Year's Day, 1962, an unknown band auditioned for Decca Records.
They recorded fifteen songs in about an hour.
Decca said no. As the story goes, they were told guitar groups were on their way out.
That band was The Beatles.
Months later, they signed with another label and became the best-selling band in history.
How many opportunities do we turn down without knowing it?

shorts.title: Michael Jordan Almost Signed With Adidas 👟
shorts.description: In 1984, Michael Jordan didn't even want to meet Nike. His mother convinced him to go.
sources: Nike annual reports — Jordan Brand revenue

scenes.text: Michael Jordan didn't want to sign with Nike. He wanted Adidas.
In 1984, Nike was mostly a running brand, not a basketball one.
Jordan didn't even want to go to the meeting. His mother convinced him.
Nike offered something almost no one got: his own shoe, and a cut of every pair sold.
That shoe was the Air Jordan. Today the Jordan brand brings in billions of dollars a year.
And Jordan still gets paid on every pair. Would you have taken the meeting?

shorts.title: When One Flower Cost as Much as a House 🌷
shorts.description: Tulip mania in 1637 Holland is often called the first speculative bubble in history.
sources: Anne Goldgar, 'Tulipmania' (2007) — on how big the crash really was

scenes.text: In the sixteen hundreds, in Holland, a single tulip bulb could cost as much as a house.
Tulips were the ultimate luxury. Everyone wanted them.
People started buying bulbs just to sell them for more a few days later.
According to accounts from the time, the rarest bulbs reached thousands of guilders.
Then, in February 1637, buyers simply stopped showing up. Prices collapsed.
It's often called the first bubble in history. Sound familiar?

shorts.title: He Failed 5,126 Times Before Getting Rich
shorts.description: James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes of his bagless vacuum cleaner.

scenes.text: This man failed five thousand one hundred and twenty six times.
James Dyson was annoyed that his vacuum lost power as the bag filled up.
So he tried to build a vacuum with no bag at all.
For about five years, he built prototype after prototype. He went deep into debt.
Prototype number five thousand one hundred and twenty seven worked.
Today Dyson is a global brand. How many times would you have tried?

shorts.title: IKEA Was Started by a 17-Year-Old
shorts.description: Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA in 1943. Do you know what the name means?
sources: Wikipedia: IKEA — name origin and flat-pack furniture

scenes.text: IKEA was started by a seventeen year old.
As a kid in Sweden, Ingvar Kamprad sold matches to his neighbors from his bike.
In 1943, he started his own company. The name is made of his initials, his family farm, and his village.
Ingvar Kamprad, Elmtaryd, Agunnaryd.
First he sold pens and wallets. Then furniture.
And the big idea came when an employee took the legs off a table to fit it in a car. Flat-pack furniture was born.

shorts.title: Red Bull Is Actually From Thailand 🐂
shorts.description: A toothpaste marketer tried a Thai energy drink on a business trip. The rest is history.
sources: Wikipedia: Red Bull — Dietrich Mateschitz and Chaleo Yoovidhya

scenes.text: Red Bull wasn't invented in Austria.
Dietrich Mateschitz was selling toothpaste. On a trip to Thailand, he tried a drink truck drivers used to stay awake.
It was called Krating Daeng. In Thai, that means red bull.
He partnered with its creator, Chaleo Yoovidhya, and changed the recipe for western tastes.
In 1987, Red Bull launched in Austria, with almost no normal ads. Just extreme sports and wild events.
Today it sells billions of cans every year.

shorts.title: LEGO Started With Wooden Ducks 🦆
shorts.description: A carpenter, a fire, and a bet on plastic: the story of LEGO.

scenes.text: LEGO started with wooden ducks.
In 1932, a Danish carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen was struggling to find work.
So he made wooden toys. The name comes from the Danish leg godt, which means play well.
In 1942, a fire burned his factory down. He rebuilt it.
Then he bet on plastic bricks, when almost nobody believed in plastic toys.
Today, LEGO is one of the biggest toy companies on Earth.

shorts.title: MySpace Went From $580M to $35M
shorts.description: In 2005, MySpace was the biggest social network on Earth. Six years later, it sold for pocket change.
sources: Wikipedia: Myspace — News Corp acquisition 2005, sale to Specific Media 2011

scenes.text: In 2005, MySpace was the biggest social network in the world.
Rupert Murdoch's News Corp bought it for five hundred and eighty million dollars.
Then Facebook showed up. Cleaner, faster, simpler.
Users left by the millions.
In 2011, MySpace sold for about thirty five million.
It lost over ninety percent of its value in six years. On the internet, nobody is untouchable.

shorts.title: $1.75 Billion App Dead in 6 Months
shorts.description: Quibi raised $1.75 billion and shut down the same year it launched.
sources: Wikipedia: Quibi — launch April 2020, shutdown announced October 2020

scenes.text: This company raised one point seven five billion dollars and died in about six months.
It was called Quibi. Hollywood-quality shows in ten minute episodes, made only for your phone.
It had stars, famous directors, and a huge budget.
It launched in April 2020, right when everyone was stuck at home, with no commute to fill.
And you couldn't even share clips on social media.
In October, it announced it was shutting down. Money can't buy success.

shorts.title: She Fooled Everyone With One Drop of Blood 🩸
shorts.description: Theranos was once worth $9 billion. Its founder ended up in prison.
sources: Wikipedia: Elizabeth Holmes — convicted January 2022, sentenced November 2022

scenes.text: She convinced the world she had a revolutionary invention. It didn't work.
Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford and started Theranos at nineteen.
She promised hundreds of medical tests from a single drop of blood.
Famous investors poured in money. At its peak, the company was valued at nine billion dollars.
But the machines didn't do what she claimed.
In 2022, she was convicted of fraud and sentenced to more than eleven years in prison.

shorts.title: Airbnb Survived by Selling Cereal 🥣
shorts.description: In 2008, Airbnb's founders were broke. Election-themed cereal boxes kept them alive.
sources: Paul Graham / Y Combinator accounts of the 2008 cereal boxes

scenes.text: Airbnb was saved by boxes of cereal.
In 2008, its founders were in debt, and almost nobody was using their website.
It was election year in America. So they designed cereal boxes for the candidates: Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's.
They sold them as collector's items.
They made about thirty thousand dollars. Just enough to keep going.
Today Airbnb is worth tens of billions. Sometimes, to survive, you have to get creative.

shorts.title: He Was So Rich He Crashed the Price of Gold 👑
shorts.description: Mansa Musa, king of Mali, is often called the richest person in history.
sources: Al-Umari's account of Musa's visit to Cairo

scenes.text: The richest person in history wasn't Elon Musk.
Many historians say it was Mansa Musa, king of the Mali Empire, in the fourteenth century.
In 1324, he traveled to Mecca with a huge caravan carrying gold.
When he passed through Cairo, he spent and gave away so much gold…
that gold lost value in the city for years.
He was so rich, nobody can really calculate his fortune.

shorts.title: Apple Fired Steve Jobs… Then Paid $429M to Get Him Back
shorts.description: In 1985, Steve Jobs was pushed out of his own company. In 1997, Apple bought his new one.
sources: Wikipedia: Steve Jobs — 1985 departure from Apple
Wikipedia: NeXT — acquired by Apple for $429 million

scenes.text: Steve Jobs was pushed out of the company he started.
In 1985, after a power struggle with Apple's CEO, the board sided against him. He left.
He started a new computer company called NeXT, and bought a small animation studio called Pixar.
Meanwhile, Apple was in serious trouble.
So Apple bought NeXT for four hundred and twenty nine million dollars, and Jobs came back.
Then came the iPod, the iPhone, and one of the most valuable companies on Earth. Getting fired can be the start.
